newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Bundesbank's Welteke says Euro currency now inevitable.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank's Welteke says Euro currency now inevitable.

text.p: Moves to create a common European currency have reached the point of no return, and any attempt to delay things would hurt the German economy, Bundesbank board member Ernst Welteke told a Moscow news conference on Friday.

"I think the point of no return has already been reached, I think we will start this monetary union on January 1, 1999," said Welteke, who is president of the regional central bank in the German state of Hesse.
"It's then a political decision," he added, referring to the first countries to introduce a single currency, to be called the euro.

Welteke, who was visiting Moscow to meet officials from the central bank and the State Duma lower house of parliament, said capital markets were already pointing to a core of European Union countries which would be able to introduce the euro from the beginning.

"If you look at the convergence of interest rates, the capital markets have already decided which states will join at the start -- Belgium, Netherlands, Luxembourg, Germany, France and Austria," he said.
Under these criteria, Ireland, Denmark and Finland would be the next candidates to join, he said.
But Welteke admitted that politics would play a major role

"I do not know what the politicians will decide," he said. "I know that Italy wants to become a member of EMU from the beginning... But on the other side Germany fears that they do not have a sound fiscal policy."
European Union member states have agreed that countries meeting certain economic criteria will introduce the euro in 1999, phasing out their domestic currencies in 2002.
Welteke said that any set-back to the EMU timetable would hurt the German economy by pushing up the mark.

"We must assume that it would lead to a revaluation of the mark and that would have a negative influence on the export capabilities of the German economy and that at a time when unemployment is already high," he said.

He said one possible approach would be to set a date between the planned introduction of the euro in 1999 and the planned abolition of national currencies in 2002 for what he described as "second-stage states" to join the currency club.
"My feeling is that there will at least be an agreement with these second-stage states that they can join EMU in two years time (after the start) before the exchange of cash happens," he said.
"That would also be a solution of the problem with Italy, Spain and Portugal."

One debate within the European Union is whether tough criteria laid down in the Maastricht Treaty should be relaxed to allow a larger number of countries to introduce a single currency from the beginning.

Germany's Handelsblatt business newspaper said in a survey published on Friday that financial experts were becoming increasingly confident that European economic and monetary union (EMU) would start as scheduled in 1999.

Experts polled by the paper said concern that many European Union members might not meet the tough fiscal criteria and qualify for EMU in the first round were becoming less important in light of political commitment to the euro.
